Ye Thought Evil Against Me, But God Meant It Unto Good
YEE THAWT EE-vul uh-GENST mee but GOD MENT it UN-too GUUD
n. phr. (Joseph's word to his brethren, Genesis 50:20)
Hebrew 'attem chashabtem 'ālay rā'āh 'elōhīm chashābāh l'tōbāh — one verb, chāshab, to devise or purpose, is used of both parties; the AV varies the English, rendering it first ‘thought’ and then ‘meant’, but the Hebrew makes the parallel exact.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jacob is buried and the brothers, afraid that Joseph has only been waiting for their father to die, send a message and then fall before his face offering themselves as servants. Joseph weeps and answers, Fear not: for am I in the place of God? — and then names what they did and what God did: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. The Hebrew uses one verb for both clauses, so that the brothers' devising and God's devising are set in deliberate parallel over a single set of events. This is the Bible's plainest statement of concurrence: the same act is genuinely the brothers' crime and genuinely God's work, without the crime ceasing to be crime or the work ceasing to be good. Joseph does not say that God made the best of a bad business, nor that the evil was secretly good. He says they meant it for evil and are guilty of it, and that God meant the identical event for good and accomplished it. The pattern is repeated at Calvary, where Peter tells Jerusalem that Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and in the same breath that they took Him and by wicked hands crucified and slew Him. Both halves are required, and neither is permitted to swallow the other.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Mean, to intend; to purpose; to design. Evil, that which produces pain, calamity, or moral wrong. Genesis 50:20, the brothers' design and God's design over one event.

expand to see more

Mean, to have in the mind; to intend; to purpose; to design.

Evil, having bad qualities of a moral kind; wicked; corrupt.

Good, that which contributes to the benefit and happiness of men.

Hebrew chāshab, to think, devise, reckon, purpose — used of both parties.

Save alive, to preserve from death. Genesis 50:20.

Key Scripture

Gen 50:19 — "And Joseph said unto them, Fear not: for am I in the place of God?"

Gen 50:20 — "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive."

Gen 45:5 — "Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life."

Act 2:23 — "Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:"

Modern Corruption

The verse is flattened into the maxim that everything happens for a reason, which excuses the brothers; or God's hand is reduced to reaction, so that He redeems a situation He did not ordain.

expand to see more

The sentimental use of this verse is the modern proverb that all things work out in the end, which comforts no one who has been genuinely wronged because it quietly tells them that the wrong was not so bad. Joseph says the opposite. Ye thought evil is an indictment, delivered to the men's faces, and they are on the ground in front of him when he says it. The verse does not dissolve guilt into providence; it holds the two together and lets the guilty go free on the ground of mercy, not on the ground that nothing really happened.

The opposite corruption is now the more common in evangelical teaching: God did not intend Joseph's pit or his prison, but He is very good at redeeming what others ruin. The grammar forbids it. The same verb governs both clauses, and Joseph had already told his brothers in Genesis 45 that it was not they that sent him thither but God. Open theism must deny this verse outright; the broader instinct that will not let God ordain what men do wickedly must at least silence it. The doctrine to recover is concurrence — that God ordains the end and the means without becoming the author of sin, and that the clearest proof is a cross which was at once the determinate counsel of God and the worst act in human history.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chāshab, to devise or purpose, governs both clauses — one event, two intentions, the brothers guilty and God good.

expand to see more

Hebrew chāshab, to think, plan, devise, impute.

The verb is identical in both halves; the AV varies the English only.

Hebrew rā'āh, evil or calamity; tōbāh, good.

Am I in the place of God? — Joseph refuses the office of avenger, Genesis 50:19.

The same double intention appears at the cross, Acts 2:23.

Usage

"ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good"

"to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive"

"it was not you that sent me hither, but God"
